motivations: Keeping their parent safe and comfortable, and sparing them suffering: worry about falls, not eating, wounds, or a home that is no longer safe.
Doing the right thing and not carrying guilt or blame: duty to a parent, fear of not doing enough, being the one who has to step up.
Love, loyalty and promises: not wanting to abandon a parent, not ready to say goodbye, keeping a promise made years ago.
Letting the parent stay at home and keep making their own choices, even when it is risky.
Honoring the parent's wishes and making the time they have left count.
Taking the load off the other parent, who is the main caregiver.
situational goals: Understand what is happening and what to do next: is this dementia or a side effect, what is normal, how others handled it.
Get help, relief or services: respite, more in-home help, approval for long-term care, someone who can step in.
Get the parent's money, bills and legal papers under control: power of attorney, Medicaid, bills paid twice, whether the parent can still sign.
Keep the parent safe and know they are OK: alone at home, falls, scams, a new facility where no one speaks up for them.
Find, choose and pay for the right place: memory care that accepts Medicaid, moving a parent closer or across states.
Get medicines right: taken on time, refused, side effects, refills.
Get the parent to accept care and look after their own health.
Handle the parent's moods and behavior without a fight.
life goals: Keep their own health and sanity: sleep, stress, not falling apart.
Keep their own life, job and money: career, studies, savings, not losing their income.
Get time and breaks for themselves, without feeling guilty.
Protect their own marriage, children and family.
Not be alone in it, and be seen by others.
Have a life and a home of their own after caregiving.

motivations: Love, loyalty and their vows: staying by their partner's side and wanting to spend the rest of their life together.
Keeping their partner safe, comfortable and with dignity, and sparing them suffering.
Keeping their partner at home, with the friends and pleasures they still enjoy.
situational goals: Get help, relief or services: someone to stay with the partner, hospice, veterans' or other programs.
Understand what is happening and what to do: what to expect next, how others handle it.
Find, choose and pay for the right place: tour memory care, join waitlists, find a way to pay.
Keep the partner safe and know the care was done: walking off, driving, blood pressure, aides doing their job.
Make sense of money and insurance: keeping coverage and doctors, getting paid as a caregiver.
Keep medicines manageable: fewer pills, quality of life first.
life goals: Keep their own health and sanity: get through each day, cope, get help for their own anxiety and depression.
Keep their own life, job and money: keep working, have a life left afterward.
Companionship, closeness and someone who understands: they feel alone in the marriage.
Get time to themselves and real breaks.
